name: Alamandine
lead: Alamandine is a heptapeptide of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), the hormone network that regulates blood pressure, fluid and electrolyte balance. It was characterised in 2013 and is formed from angiotensin A by ACE2, or directly from angiotensin-(1-7).[1][5]

It acts mainly through the MrgD receptor and, in laboratory studies, produces effects that oppose those of angiotensin II, such as vasorelaxation and protection against cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis in animals.[1][5] Published work is preclinical; no human clinical trial of alamandine as a treatment was found.[5]

Alamandine is listed among peptides grouped in the longevity category in some compound catalogues. The only route from it to a better physique or appearance is the one researchers describe in animal work: anti-fibrotic, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions in tissues such as heart, vessels, lung and bone, which are discussed as protective of tissue structure.[4][11] No source documents use of alamandine for appearance.

paras: Alamandine has the sequence Ala-Arg-Val-Tyr-Ile-His-Pro and a molar mass of about 855 g/mol [5]. It differs from angiotensin-(1-7) by having alanine in place of aspartic acid at the amino end [5]. It forms through ACE2-dependent hydrolysis of angiotensin A, which is itself made from angiotensin II by decarboxylation in mononuclear leukocytes, or by decarboxylation of the aspartic acid residue of angiotensin-(1-7) [5]. A 2007 report by Jankowski and colleagues had detected angiotensin A in human circulation at higher levels in people with end-stage renal disease [5].

The 2013 Circulation Research paper reported identification of alamandine by mass spectrometry, showed that it circulates in human blood, and described its generation by ACE2 from angiotensin A or from angiotensin-(1-7).[1] Wikipedia notes that an earlier 2007 report had detected the peptide in human plasma.[5]

Reviews place alamandine in the protective arm of the RAS alongside ACE2, angiotensin-(1-7) and the Mas receptor, whose actions generally counteract angiotensin II in the heart, kidney and vasculature.[2][4][7] A 2014 review described it as a vasoactive peptide with actions similar to angiotensin-(1-7) acting through MrgD, a counter-regulatory mechanism within the RAS [8]. Related work examines the MAS-related receptor family to which MrgD belongs.[3]

Alamandine acts on the MrgD receptor. Wikipedia reports that vasorelaxation by alamandine was blocked by an MrgD antagonist but not by the Mas antagonist A779, and that in cells expressing MrgD it increased cAMP [5]. Mice lacking MrgD developed dilated cardiomyopathy with a marked drop in systolic function, which supports a cardioprotective role for the pathway [5].

According to the encyclopedia summary of the literature, alamandine produced endothelium-dependent vessel relaxation, lowered blood pressure in spontaneously hypertensive rats, and reduced cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis in mice under pressure overload [5]. In a transverse aortic constriction mouse model it reduced arterial remodelling and lowered inflammatory markers including IL-1 beta, TNF-alpha and TGF beta1 [5].

A 2021 study in mice with the same pressure-overload model reported that alamandine improved cardiac remodelling [9], and a 2024 mouse study reported that it attenuated oxidative stress in the carotid artery [12]. A 2022 review describes alamandine as a promising anti-fibrotic agent that modulates inflammation and collagen deposition and acts as an antioxidant, with particular interest in post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis [4]; a 2021 review discusses potential protective effects in SARS-CoV-2 patients [13]. A 2024 rat study examined alamandine in monocrotaline-induced pulmonary hypertension [14], and a 2024 study reported that alamandine attenuated ovariectomy-induced osteoporosis in a mouse model by promoting osteogenic differentiation [15]. All of these are cell and animal data.

Alamandine has no approved human use. Peptide catalogues place it among longevity-category research peptides, and a CNS microinjection study reported that placing alamandine in the insular cortex of animals raised blood pressure, illustrating that effects differ by tissue and route [5]. No community discussion of alamandine for physique or looks was found.

No studies found. Published research on alamandine consists of laboratory and animal studies; the encyclopedia entry reports higher circulating angiotensin A levels in people with end-stage renal disease, which is an observation rather than a treatment trial.[5]

card.summary: A blood-pressure-regulating peptide of the renin-angiotensin system; interesting cardiovascular biology in rodents, no human trials.
card.note: Preclinical only; no human therapeutic data.

quick.overview:
Alamandine is a small peptide made in the body as part of the renin-angiotensin system. It was described in 2013 and appears to counterbalance the blood-pressure-raising arm of that system.

Evidence for any effect comes from cell and rodent experiments. It is listed among longevity-category peptides, but no human trials have tested it.
quick.mechanism: It is generated by ACE2 from angiotensin A (or from angiotensin-(1-7)) and signals mainly through the MrgD receptor, producing vasorelaxation and anti-fibrotic effects in animals.[1][5]
quick.risks: No human safety data exist. Because it influences blood pressure and vascular tone in animals, effects in people are unstudied. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: Alamandine appears in longevity-peptide lists because it opposes angiotensin II-driven fibrosis and inflammation in rodents. These findings concern heart, vessel, lung and bone tissue, not appearance, and no human use is documented.
